Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy
Proposal · intraoperative level counting · September 2026

Counting the vertebral level under fluoroscopy, without a tracker

Prepared for Dr. Chou and the department. One method, one number it produces, what it has been measured to do, where synthetic training data stops, and what the retrospective fluoroscopy in our PACS would let it guarantee.

TL;DR, for the surgeon and the CFO. Wrong-level spine surgery is 1 in 830 operations in a 34,544-case registry (1 in 240 in the thoracic spine), and half of surveyed spine surgeons have done it once; 81% of events are a count that went wrong under fluoroscopy. This method counts the level on the C-arm the hospital already owns — no tracker, no capital purchase — and is exact on 99.2–100% of walks when its boxes are right. The dollars that can be priced are operating-room minutes (about ten a case, $140k–$500k a year at 300–1,000 cases); the never event is a harm and a reputation, not a line item. The one number no synthetic or cadaver data can predict is how it performs on our machines and patients, which is what the retrospective collection below measures. The one-page version with every source.

The proposal is to count, not to name. A C-arm sweep from an anchor the surgeon already trusts (the sacrum, or C2) to the level in hand, frame by frame, with each vertebra linked to the last by its image and the count read off the chain. The only learned component finds vertebral bodies and the anchor in a frame; nothing learned decides the level. The count is exact wherever the boxes are right, and the deployment question is therefore a detection question, which is what this document is about.

1. The method, in one line

1 · exposeAnchor at the edge of the first field: sacrum or C2.
2 · detectVertebral bodies and the anchor class in each frame. The one learned stage.
3 · linkConsecutive overlapping frames matched by normalised cross-correlation, restricted to within 0.6 of a body of the commanded step.
4 · chainA panorama with every body a node.
5 · countThe target is the k-th node from the anchor. No name is formed; no alphabet is needed.

2. How well it counts, in domain

Measured on public labelled CT renders and real radiographs, with the annotation's vertebra boxes, so that the count is tested on its own terms. A walk is exact when the mark lands on the body truly k from the anchor, scored among walks that reached the target.

Twelve arms of 16 to 801 spines each lie between 99.17 and 100%. Exactness is regional: 99.7% lumbar and 95.5% thoracic from the sacrum; 83.8% cervical in the one arm that reaches that far.

3. Where the level is, on the map

A confirming exposure with the instrument on bone is placed on the map by its count, and the body it touches is marked. The instrument here is rendered as what a steel cylinder does to a path-length integral — densest on its axis, tapering at the bevel, blurred by the receptor and edged by the enhancement like every cortex in the frame — not drawn on top.

4. The learned stage on real radiographs

The deployed film detector was trained on annotated real plain films. On films it was not trained on, lumbar and cervical, its calls sit on the annotation's boxes; the misses it does make are the whole deployment risk, because a missed body is a miscount.

Thin green: the annotation. Red: the detector's calls at confidence 0.25 with scores. One cervical film loses its lowest body; one carries an extra call. Recall on real film: 99.14% per body for the film-trained detector; 71.67% for the same architecture trained on renders only.

5. What synthetic fluoroscopy from CT can do, and where it stops

Fluoroscopy is not plain film: different grain, window, scatter, collimation, exposure per view, and no annotated public corpus of intraoperative frames. So the renderer was calibrated on the one public set that pairs real C-arm frames with their CT and exact pose — DeepFluoro, 366 frames of six cadaveric pelves on a Siemens Cios Fusion — and a detector trained only on calibrated renders was tested on the real frames.

The physics is close

Exact geometry (0.00 px) and polyenergetic attenuation explain 81% of a real frame's variance; nine calibrated device terms add +4; a per-frame smooth field (the device's window, scatter pedestal, heel, vignette) brings it to 93.9% against a quantum-noise ceiling of 99.5%. What remains below 8 px is under one percent of variance per band, at cortical edges the 1 mm CT does not resolve.

The population is not

A detector trained on renders of DeepFluoro's own CTs finds the sacrum on 90–97% of the real frames, six specimens held out in turn. The same detector trained on renders of living whole-body CTs finds it on 64–77%. The renderer is not what limits it; embalmed pelves surrounded by air are not living abdomens, and the labels are not the same labels.

What learning adds

A RealDRR-style refiner trained on the real pairs, a high-pass-only version of it, and a training-free low-band swap were each trained six folds by three seeds and applied to the living-abdomen renders. Measured on all six folds, three seeds each, against the same baseline on the same folds: the Fourier low-band swap added about ten points, the high-pass refiner and the full refiner about eight — all the same sign, each smaller than the 26-point seed spread, none within fifteen points of the population-matched control. Applied to that control’s own renders the same refiners added two to five points. Every refiner beat identity on its validation specimen, yet on the 366 held-out real frames the refined render agrees with the real frame slightly less than the plain calibrated one (68.1% against 69.3% of display variance explained; better on only one frame in five). It sharpens and it invents; the detector gains from the first and the pixels pay for the second. Where the calibrated render is wrong is now measured by region, with the collimator border kept separate: the border ring, a fifth of the field, holds about two thirds of the residual, because the real frame falls off through the penumbra and the render stops at a hard edge; inside it, cortical edges agree with the real frame to within a few grey levels at every bone thickness. A thin-bone deficit reported earlier was that border counted as a bone edge, and it has been withdrawn. The stored DeepFluoro frames also turned out to be log-compressed display images; read correctly, physics alone explains 86% of a real frame rather than 80%, and the calibrated renderer about 90% of a held-out one.

The limits, stated. Every number above is tuned to one C-arm, one protocol and one specimen population. Three training seeds of one dataset spanned 26 points on one specimen, so single-run differences between methods do not exist. Only the sacrum has a per-structure truth in DeepFluoro; the vertebrae are one merged class. And the best synthetic frame still sits 13–30 points below the in-domain result on the same population — that gap is the cost of not having real, annotated, in-domain fluoroscopy.

6. The proposal: our own fluoroscopy, retrospectively

Dr. Chou's spine cases save their intraoperative fluoroscopy to PACS. Five years of it is the in-domain corpus this method has never had: the same C-arms, the same technologists' habits, the same patient population it would be used on, with the operative level known from the record.

Collection

A retrospective protocol (existing clinical images; waiver of consent; de-identification of headers and burned-in text at export). Every saved fluoroscopic series from spine cases, 2021–2026, with the operative levels and approach from the operative note, and post-operative imaging where it exists as the level truth.

Annotation

A subset of cases annotated for vertebral bodies, the sacrum or C2 anchor, and instrument-on-bone frames — the three things the method consumes — by the same protocol as the film corpus. The rest held out by case, never by frame, as the test.

Measurement

Per-body recall of the detector on held-out cases; exactness of the count against the record; the decline rate at each operating point; and the audit trail — every case's chain, frame by frame — so a wrong count can be traced to the frame that caused it.

What to expect

The evidence for the prediction is the population-matched control above: when the training renders are of the test population, the same detector finds the sacrum on 90–97% of real frames; when the population is real film of the kind it was trained on, per-body recall is 99.14%. Fine-tuned on a few thousand annotated in-domain frames, the fluoroscopy detector should reach the film detector's range on held-out cases from the same devices; the count adds essentially nothing to that error (99.2–100% exact given the boxes). The number that cannot be predicted from cadaver or synthetic data is the one this collection exists to measure: the per-case wrong-level rate on our own patients, with our own machines.

What it can guarantee

  • Not a fixed accuracy. A measured bound on wrong-level output at a stated decline rate, on held-out cases, re-measured whenever the device, protocol or population changes.
  • Refusal, not a guess. When a frame fails to link, or the anchor is not found, the system declines that walk; a decline is a repeat exposure, not a wrong level. The guarantee is that wrong answers are converted into declines at a rate the operator chooses.
  • An audit trail per case. The chain of frames, the boxes and the count are stored; any disagreement with the record is traceable to a frame.
  • No name is formed. The method never asserts "L4"; it asserts "four from the sacrum". Transitional anatomy is counted the same way it is operated on.

7. Start this week: the WSU C-arm, a phantom, and a cadaver

Feasibility from the operator's side — can a person execute the sweep on a real C-arm, and does the linker hold on real detector output — does not need patient data. Wayne State's C-arm fluoroscope in 0312 Elliman (Division of Laboratory Animal Resources) is available to trained users, and every prerequisite has a fixed lead time of fifteen business days, so the paperwork is the critical path.

Before the room (15 business days)

OEHS online Radiation Generating Machine refresher; Laboratory Specific Training Form (Appendix L) with the DLAR Director's certification, filed in the 0312 log book; Dosimetry Request Form signed by the DLAR Director (313-577-9479) to Health Physics, 5425 Woodward Suite 300 (313-577-1200); whole-body, collar and ring badges received by DLAR; RSC protocol approval for a phantom study (IACUC only if animal tissue is used); 0.5 mm lead aprons for everyone in the room.

Phantom sweeps

An anthropomorphic lumbar spine phantom on a radiolucent table; the C-arm's video output through a lossless frame grabber into a laptop; anchor at the sacrum, commanded steps of one field minus two bodies, overlapping exposures; the linker and detector run live; the count checked against the phantom. This calibrates the frame grabber, the step protocol and the operator's hand, and gives the first real detector-output frames from a WSU machine.

Cadaver, then the OR

The Body Bequest Program (Barb Rosso-Norgan, 313-577-1188, brosso@med.wayne.edu) supplies whole-body donors for research on a proposal; cadaver work is not human-subjects research and needs no IRB, only the program's and biosafety approval. Prone on a radiolucent table: anchor, sweep, instrument on bone, confirming frame — the full protocol on true tissue, scale and scatter, with the renderer's DeepFluoro calibration checked against this machine's frames.

Asks: access to the PACS series for the retrospective protocol; the operative notes for level truth; ten to twenty hours of annotation by a resident under the existing protocol; and one C-arm session to record the device's calibration frames (a step wedge and a pose phantom), so the renderer can be tuned to our machines the way it was tuned to DeepFluoro's.
